extraction_notes: Extracted from catalogs/windsor-school/catalog_2026-27.pdf (63 pages; no low-text pages). The 2025-26 catalog was not needed. Phase 1 notes the 2026-27 document is possibly a draft (metadata title "In Progress"; table of contents header and several internal labels still say 2025/2026). The separate grad_requirements_2026-27.pdf (2 pages) repeats the catalog page 4 table but lists Swarm (.25 credit/year) instead of Junior Seminar/Capstone; used to enrich notes only. Catalog marks nearly every course "*Semester" even when 1-2 credits; where credits >= 1 and no other length statement exists, length is "unknown" (set to "year" only where the text says year-long/full year/broken into two semesters or the title says Full Year). Description lines containing right-hand sidebar notes were split by column. "Design & Technology" is listed in both Computer & Technology (p38) and Fine Arts (p47) with identical text: one record. "Theater Arts: Creative Movement" appears in PE (p43) and Fine Arts (p47) with different descriptions: one record (PE text), other listing noted in notes. World Studies I/II and Psychology I/II share one description each: kept as one record each. Algebra A / Algebra B split into two records. Remaining check warnings are false positives caused by the right-hand sidebar (prerequisite/notes column) being interleaved with the description in both text files: Genetics and Evolution (possible dropped text; description also straddles a page break) and World Literature (not verbatim); descriptions were copied from the left column only and compared with the PDF layout. HACTC programs are listed by name only (15 records, level CTE) with embedded credit in fulfills_text; the catalog also says juniors/seniors may apply. Flexible Pathways options (dual enrollment, early college, virtual learning, ELO, focused pathway electives, CBL, WBL, independent study) recorded as program records. RVCC dual-enrollment courses are recorded within their departments with level dual_enrollment.

courses.description: introduces students to the major genres of literature. English 9 is based around questions arising from the role of the individual in the community: questions of personal identity, individual freedom, civil rights, and the role of the individual citizen in the larger community. Students will work on basic skills in vocabulary, grammar, writing, and reading.

This course is designed for freshmen who love to read and write and would like the opportunity for a more challenging course. English 9 Intensive allows students to move at a quicker pace, choose higher-level literature, and engage in deeper discussions. Some reading will be expected to be done outside of class and may include up to 25 pages in a night. Essays and stories that involve several drafts will also require work outside of class; however, class time will be allotted as well. Common Core State Standard-aligned short stories, poems, and novels of challenge and rigor will be read throughout the course.
courses.notes: Intensive (more challenging) version of English 9

courses.description: Students will explore short stories, plays, movies, novels, and poetry from Latin America, Africa, Russia, and Asia as they analyze how culture and conflict are portrayed in literature and film. Students will reflect upon the materials through analytical, personal, and creative responses. During the 10th grade year, there will be a strong integration between the historical topics covered in World Studies and the readings in World Literature. Class discussions and larger-scale projects will also be incorporated into the course curriculum. Common Core State Standard-aligned materials will be studied throughout the course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9

courses.description: Students will explore short stories, plays, movies, novels, and poetry from Latin America, Africa, Russia, and Asia as they analyze how culture and conflict are portrayed in literature and film. Students will reflect upon the materials through analytical, personal, and creative responses. This course is designed for students who enjoy reading and writing and would like the opportunity for a more challenging approach. Some reading and writing may be expected to be done outside of class. However, class time will always be provided as well. Common Core State Standard-aligned materials will be studied throughout the course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9
courses.notes: Intensive (more challenging) version of World Literature

courses.description: This course is devoted to a study of American literature. Modern American Literature will focus on the time period between the mid-late 1800s to around the mid-1900s. Students will have the opportunity to read a variety of works from notable American authors, including diverse voices from the 19th and 20th centuries. Students will read fiction and nonfiction texts, as well as find and make connections with history, art and other subjects. Students will be expected to read independently, write analytically, and contribute to class discussions.

This course is devoted to a study of American literature. Postmodern American Literature will focus on the time period from the 1950s to present day. Students will have the opportunity to read a variety of works from notable American authors, including diverse voices from the 20th and 21st centuries. Students will read fiction and nonfiction texts, as well as find and make connections with history, art and other subjects. Students will be expected to read independently, write analytically, and contribute to class discussions.

Creative Writing introduces students to the process of writing short stories, poetry, plays, and memoirs, while also allowing them to explore a larger, semester-long writing project of their own choosing. Using a workshop structure, students will engage in creative writing exercises, revise and edit their own work, and critique the work of others. Time will also be dedicated each week to independent reading selections, which will be chosen by each individual student. It is an expectation of the course that students will share their work with each other, and that they will provide constructive feedback to their peers.

This course is a study of the important writers in speculative fiction (Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Horror), including Arthur C. Clarke, Philip K. Dick, Neil Gaiman, Ray Bradbury, Ursula Le Guin, J.R.R. Tolkien and H.G. Wells, H.P. Lovecraft, Octavia E. Butler, Bram Stoker, Mary Shelly, and Steven King. The course focuses on what these genres can tell us about the times that produced them and changing ideas about important social concepts such as heroes, honor, and good and evil.

Literature of War explores a variety of ways in which literature, film, and music deal with the subject of war. The focus of the course is on 20th century conflicts, including but not limited to World War I, the Irish Civil War, World War II, and Vietnam. Short stories, novels, and films are all incorporated to deepen students’ understanding of each unique war and conflict, and of the experiences particular to those events. Realistic, dramatic, musical, and comedic depictions of the subject matter will be incorporated in the course. Reflective, analytical, and creative responses will be used.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9

courses.description: Mythology has been integral to cultures around the world and throughout history, helping provide answers to lifelong questions and inspiring behavior and storytelling. In this course, students will take a comparative approach to exploring the myths and beliefs of world cultures, including Greek, Norse and British. We will read Beowulf, about King Arthur, and other literature inspired by myths. Studies will focus on concepts of the hero, creation, love and family. We will investigate the following questions: What do myths reveal about a culture? What effect do myths have, then and now?

Sports Literature focuses on the impact of sports in both American and international culture. Readings will include fictional short stories, topical essays, and other non-fiction writing. Students will also be exposed to films inspired by sports and athletes, and will examine how and why sports have become such a significant part of our culture. Topics range from the traditional (greatest sports rivalries, fighting in hockey, PEDs in sport), to the non-traditional (big-wave surfing, extreme sports), with plenty of stops in between.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9

courses.description: Literature and Artistic Expression is a choice-driven course where students are provided with the opportunity to select and read works of literature that appeal to their own personal tastes and interests, and to explore and expand upon those works through artistic expression. Such forms of expression may include (but are not limited to) the creation of paintings, drawings, poetry, cartoons, sculptures, and creative fictional pieces. Students will also reflect upon the choices they made when creating their artistic pieces.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9

courses.description: Poetry is an exploration and expression of the human experience. It is a dance with words–sometimes beautiful, sometimes frightening–and everything in between. In this semester-long elective, students will read, analyze, and write poetry while learning about its many forms and techniques. Classic and contemporary poems will be selected by both teacher and students. Students will recite poetry in class and may choose to recite for a larger audience. First-semester Poetry students will have the additional opportunity to enter the national Poetry Out Loud recitation competition.

courses.course_name: Film Studies - Focus on Story and Theme
courses.description: At the heart of a film is a good story. In this course, students will view a wide variety of classic and contemporary films to consider the question: What makes a good story? How do they help us understand the world and ourselves? We’ll consider genre, historical period, theme, plot, characterization, motifs, allusions, metaphors, and other core elements of literary analysis. We’ll also look at lighting, sound, cinematography, acting, special effects, and other elements of film analysis. Students should be prepared to analyze films through both writing and discussion.

In this course, students will read, analyze, interpret, discuss, and write about short fiction. Readings will include various forms of the story, as well as stories from different cultures, countries, and centuries. Emphasis will be on close, careful reading of text, and students will be introduced to the concepts and terminology of prose literature including plot, conflict, characterization, theme, point of view, and imagery. This is a “dual-enrollment class,” offered in conjunction with River Valley Community College. The student taking this class has the option of earning three RVCC credits (different colleges and universities that you apply to may have their own requirements for accepting transfer credits from RVCC) in addition to one Windsor High School credit English elective credit.
courses.notes: *Spring Semester; RVCC Dual Enrollment Course

courses.description: In this RVCC Dual Enrollment course, students learn to write clearly and effectively for defined audiences through a variety of writing strategies, behaviors, habits, and attitudes. Emphasis is on the writing process from pre-writing through drafting, revising, and editing. Students gain confidence through learning basic writing principles of effective expository composition and the application of these principles in writing essays and documented papers, as well as an understanding on how to use MLA and APA citation methods, which are most often used for college-level writing. Resources for this class may include texts, electronic resources, and personal experiences. This is not a basic or remedial writing class, but a college-level introductory course. This is a “dual-enrollment class,” offered in conjunction with River Valley Community College. The student taking this class has the option of earning three RVCC credits (different colleges and universities that you apply to may have their own requirements for accepting transfer credits from RVCC) in addition to one Windsor High School credit English credit.
courses.notes: *Fall Semester; RVCC Dual Enrollment Course

courses.description: In this semester-long course, students will study comics as literature, and their contribution to modern American culture. Throughout the course, students will explore long and short works like Persepolis by Marjane Satrapi, Maus by Art Spiegelman, and Watchmen by Alan Moore, along with a number of other shorter works. Students will also have the opportunity to choose comics from the Windsor Public Library to read during a number of independent units, and to explore the connection between comics and film by watching some examples of notable film adaptations. As an English class, the expectation is that students will be prepared not only to read comics and watch films, but also to examine them critically and write about them as they would in any other literature class. Please note that some of the works in this class deal with visual depictions of violence and other sensitive topics.

Civics is a required year-long course for all freshmen. Civics prepares you to be an informed and active citizen by developing your understanding of the history, principles and foundations of our American democracy, and the ability to participate in civic and democratic practices. Civics is not limited to the study of “government”; it encompasses participation in schools, our towns, groups and organizations. Our communities and our nation need citizens to be able to fully participate, and Civics lays the foundation for that. Students taking Civics will be expected to engage in a civil manner, while developing an understanding of multiple perspectives of current issues, evaluate information from a variety of news media, express ideas effectively through written communication and engage in and facilitate discussions.
courses.notes: Required year-long course for all freshmen; broken into two semesters, each awarded .5 credit (catalog labels it *Semester)

courses.description: World Studies is broken down into two semester long courses. Semester I focuses on Latin America & Africa while semester 2 focuses on Russia & Asia. These courses are centered around a comparative approach to colonization, revolution and political change. During the course students will study a variety of sources including primary and secondary sources, art, music, documentaries and film clips.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Civics or equivalent
courses.notes: World Studies I: Latin American & Africa; World Studies II Russia & Asia - two semester-long courses, each .5 credit; grade level not stated (10th-grade World Literature integrates with World Studies)

courses.description: United States History is an exploration of American society and culture starting in the 1860’s and extending to the present day. After a short review of the Civil War and Reconstruction, course content will focus on the rise of industrialism, reform movements, the emergence of the United States as a world power, World War I, the Roaring Twenties, the Great Depression, World War II, the Cold War, Vietnam, modern U.S. foreign and domestic policy, and the War in Iraq. The central themes of the course will include social, political, and economic change over time; the changing impact of ethnic, racial, and economic diversity of the nation; and the intricacies and evolution in governing the U.S. democracy.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Civics or equivalent
courses.notes: Catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit; length not clear. Catalog requires a full year of Civics & U.S. History

courses.description: Psychology is a survey course studying all aspects of human behavior and experience, including personality, child development, brain physiology, learning, perception, emotions, and psychological disorders. Students are expected to participate actively in class discussions, and must be capable of approaching sensitive issues with an appropriate level of maturity. All students can benefit from an introduction to psychology, however, this course is particularly appropriate for students considering future college studies in the humanities, education, and healthcare field. *Psych I - Fall semester will focus on introducing the approaches to Psych, understanding research design, the biology of psychology, and studying developmental psychology covering the human lifespan. *Psych II - Spring semester dives deeper into specific aspects of the field including perception, consciousness, behavioral psych, stress, psychological illness and mental health
courses.prerequisites: Psych I must be completed before taking Psych II
courses.notes: Psych I fall semester, Psych II spring semester

courses.description: The focus of this class is the development of the Western tradition leading up to the year 1500. The heart of this class will be seminar-style in-class discussions. We will be spending a significant amount of class time reading primary source material, and questioning, discussing, and debating the ideas that changed history. Among the topics and themes we will cover are the development of the first civilizations, the growth of empires, the spread of cultures, the birth of world religions, the birth of democracy, the Greek Golden Age, the Roman Empire, the Medieval Era, and the Renaissance. This is a “dual-enrollment class,” offered in conjunction with River Valley Community College. The student taking this class has the option of earning 3 college credits (that can be transferred to the college of their choice) in addition to Windsor High School credit.
courses.notes: RVCC Dual Enrollment Course; catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit

courses.course_name: The Making of the Modern World
courses.description: The focus of this class is the development of the Western tradition from the Renaissance (ca 1500) to the present. The heart of this class will be seminar-style in-class discussions. We will be spending a significant amount of class time reading primary source material, and questioning, discussing, and debating the ideas that changed history. Among the topics and themes we will cover are the Age of Exploration, the development of nation states, Imperialism, Capitalism and Communism, World Wars One and Two, and the Cold War. This is a “dual-enrollment class,” offered in conjunction with River Valley Community College. The student taking this class has the option of earning 3 college credits (that can be transferred to the college of their choice) in addition to Windsor High School credit.
courses.notes: RVCC Dual Enrollment Course; catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit

courses.description: Human Geography & Cultures is a course designed to allow students to explore the world beyond our national borders. The exact content of this course will be strongly influenced by student interest, incorporating common principles of Human, Cultural, and Physical Geography. We’ll look at how location, natural resources, and environment shaped various regions of the world, and how that geography continues to influence the people of that region.

This course examines the role that movies play in the documentation of history and how they can be used to better understand the world around us. Students will watch films across a varied assortment of eras and regions that will broaden the student’s horizon around different events throughout the course of history.

Using the Eureka math curriculum, this course is designed to provide 9th graders with a review of the topics needed to be successful in Algebra. Each section is a year long, allowing students to gain a thorough understanding of the material. Algebra A will provide many opportunities to revisit and expand the understanding of foundational algebra concepts, will employ diagnostic means to offer focused interventions, and will incorporate varied instructional strategies to prepare students for required high school courses. Particular focus is given to Integers; Order of Operations; Graphing; Polynomials and Equations; Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages; Exponents; and Word Problems. Algebra B builds off of the first course. Particular focus is given to Relationships Between Quantities and Reasoning with Equations and Their Graphs; Descriptive Statistics; Linear and Exponential Functions; Polynomial and Quadratic Expressions, Equations, and Functions; and A Synthesis of Modeling with Equations and Functions.
courses.notes: Listed as "Algebra A / Algebra B" with one description; each section is a year long. Math level based on placement test

courses.description: Using the Eureka math curriculum, this course is designed to provide 9th graders with a review of the topics needed to be successful in Algebra. Each section is a year long, allowing students to gain a thorough understanding of the material. Algebra A will provide many opportunities to revisit and expand the understanding of foundational algebra concepts, will employ diagnostic means to offer focused interventions, and will incorporate varied instructional strategies to prepare students for required high school courses. Particular focus is given to Integers; Order of Operations; Graphing; Polynomials and Equations; Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages; Exponents; and Word Problems. Algebra B builds off of the first course. Particular focus is given to Relationships Between Quantities and Reasoning with Equations and Their Graphs; Descriptive Statistics; Linear and Exponential Functions; Polynomial and Quadratic Expressions, Equations, and Functions; and A Synthesis of Modeling with Equations and Functions.
courses.notes: Listed as "Algebra A / Algebra B" with one description; each section is a year long. Math level based on placement test

courses.description: Using the Eureka math curriculum, this course is designed to provide students with an overview of Algebra concepts in five Modules. Particular focus is given to Relationships Between Quantities and Reasoning with Equations and Their Graphs; Descriptive Statistics; Linear and Exponential Functions; Polynomial and Quadratic Expressions, Equations, and Functions; and A Synthesis of Modeling with Equations and Functions.
courses.notes: Math level based on placement test

courses.description: Using the Eureka math curriculum, this course is designed to provide students with an overview of basic geometry concepts. Particular focus is given to congruency including transformations, similarity including trigonometry, measurement, circles, equations, and coordinate geometry.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (credit) of Algebra 1

courses.description: Using the Eureka math curriculum, this course is designed to provide students with an overview of basic geometry concepts. Particular focus is given to congruency including transformations, similarity including trigonometry, measurement, circles, equations, and coordinate geometry. In addition, students in the Honors Geometry will tackle geometric proofs and other challenging applications of concepts.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra I with a Standards grade of 3 or higher.

courses.description: Project Based Math (PBM) applies previous mathematical knowledge, with reinforcement, to design and implement hands-on deliverables. Students are exposed to the engineering design process and learn how to make their own technical drawings. Students immediately apply these skills to make picture frames, signage for local businesses, and homemade hydroponics. The course explores data collection and representation by logging plant growth and water nutrient levels. No skills in woodworking are required.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 1

courses.description: This course is designed to complete the third year of math for a graduation requirement. Using the Eureka curriculum, the topics introduced in Algebra I are expanded upon. Particular focus is given to polynomial and rational expressions, logarithms and exponential functions, trigonometry, and statistics. Graphing of various types of functions, calculator usage and real world applications are integral aspects of student learning. A graphing calculator (TI-83 or TI-84) is required for this course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (credit) of Algebra I and Geometry

courses.description: This course is designed for students planning to continue their math education through trigonometry and/or calculus. Using the Eureka math curriculum, the topics introduced in Algebra I are expanded upon. Particular focus is given to polynomial and rational functions, conic sections, logarithms and exponential functions, sequences and series, trigonometry, and statistics. Graphing of various types of functions, calculator usage and real world applications are integral aspects of student learning. A graphing calculator (TI-83 or TI-84) is required for this course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra I and Honors Geometry with a Standards-based grade of 3 or higher.

courses.description: This math course focuses on basic economic terms, concepts, and practical tasks such as budgeting, taxes, loans, credit, and real world problems you
courses.fulfills_text: Math; This course is now a requirement prior to graduation (starting with class of 2027)

courses.description: The statistics course is a Running Start Course (for college credit). The standard topics from a first year college statistics course are included.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 2 or Honors Algebra 2 with a Standards-based grade of 2.5 or higher.
courses.notes: Running Start course (for college credit); RVCC Dual Enrollment course; catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit

courses.description: Precalculus builds on the algebra skills from Algebra II by further exploring factoring, roots, logarithms, and higher power equations. The course focuses on analyzing functions via their domain, range, intercepts, and symmetry. Students also extend their knowledge of Trigonometry by integrating trigonometric functions into algebraic expressions. The course prepares students for Calculus by ensuring they are experts in algebra and trig.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra II

courses.description: The calculus course is the equivalent to an advanced placement course. The standard topics from a first year college calculus course are included. These topics include limits, derivatives and integrals.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Precalculus
courses.notes: RVCC Dual Enrollment course; catalog labels it *Semester but lists 2 credit

courses.description: Biology actively engages students in the study of living organisms with a strong inquiry focus. Students will spend a significant amount of time at the beginning of the year learning about how to design, evaluate and redesign scientific experiments. The topics of evolution and natural selection will be an overarching theme the entire year when studying the structure and organization of organisms from the macroscopic to microscopic scale. Topics include: Experimental Design, Classification of Organisms, Evolution and Natural Selection, Energy Processes, Cell Structure and Function, Growth and Reproduction, and Heredity and Genetics.
courses.notes: Broken into two semesters, each awarded .5 credit (catalog labels it *Semester)

courses.description: Earth & the Environment is a full year, interdisciplinary science course designed for the student interested in understanding more about the world around them and their place in it. This is a class that will challenge the student both analytically and conceptually. Major concepts will be learned through critical thinking, problem solving, decision-making, and cooperative learning. Activities, investigations, debates, discussions, and projects will provide the student with an opportunity to dig deeper into topics such as: Sustainability, Basic Earth Science, Waste Management and Recycling, Green Building, Energy, Air-Water-Soil Quality, Climate Change, Agriculture, and Population Growth.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (credit) of Biology
courses.notes: Described as a full year course

courses.description: STEM Research and Inquiry is a semester-long course designed for juniors who have completed at least two years of laboratory science and math. Each student will have the opportunity to develop a research project that he or she will have the entire semester to investigate using scientific laboratory or engineering design techniques. The student will be responsible for planning and implementing each phase of his or her project. Students will read scientific journals, develop hypotheses, collect and analyze data, perform statistical analyses, create a formal research poster and write a formal research paper. Students will present their posters at the local science fair with the hopes of attending the state and international science fairs.
courses.notes: Requirement for all juniors not enrolled in Hartford Area Career and Technical Center (HACTC); first semester of junior year

courses.description: Physical Science offers a conceptual approach to basic chemistry and physics concepts. The coursework focuses on applying these concepts to everyday experiences and has a strong inquiry focus. This course starts with the Big Bang to explain the origins of matter and the structure of atoms. After a foundation of matter is established, students then progress into energy and learn about the interaction between the two. Coursework will also familiarize students with the methods of science: experimental design, variable control, data collection and interpretation, inductive and deductive reasoning, bias, and various modes of communicating results
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology and Earth & the Environment
courses.notes: Catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit

courses.description: Chemistry offers a detailed examination of traditional chemistry topics designed for students interested in a science, health, or engineering career. The coursework is math-based with a strong inquiry focus and will challenge the student both analytically and conceptually. Major concepts will be learned through laboratory experience, critical thinking, problem-solving, and cooperative learning. Topics include Properties and Structure of Matter, Reaction Types, Stoichiometry, Equilibrium and Reaction Rates, Acids and Bases, Dilutions and Titrations, Thermochemistry, and Nuclear Chemistry. This course is intended for students interested in pursuing a career in science, health, engineering or students who plan to seek admission to competitive colleges. Participation in the school science fair is a requirement of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (credit) of Biology and Earth & the Environment and Algebra II (or concurrently)
courses.notes: Catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit

courses.description: Physics is designed to prepare students who are considering a career in science or engineering. The course starts in space, exploring the origins of matter and its interactions with energy at the atomic scale. The course then zooms out from the atomic scale to the human scale to study larger interactions between matter and energy. The course will be math-based and will address the content on the Physics SAT subject test. Topics will include Kinematics, Dynamics, Energy & Momentum, Circular Motion, and Gravity, Heat & Thermodynamics, Fluids, Electricity & Magnetism, Simple Harmonics, Waves & Optics, and Modern Physics. Participation in the school science fair is a requirement of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology, Earth & the Environment and Algebra II. May run concurrently
courses.notes: Catalog labels it *Semester but lists 1 credit

courses.description: Human Biology explores the structure and function of the major systems of the human body. This course is targeted for students interested in pursuing a career in a medical-related field. Rigorous and fast paced, this year-long course will include topics such as: medical terminology, tissue types, and the skeletal, muscular, nervous, digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine, urinary and reproductive systems. This is a “dual-enrollment class,” offered in conjunction with River Valley Community College. The student taking this class has the option of earning 3 college credits (that can be transferred to the college of their choice) in addition to Windsor High School credit.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology & Chemistry (or concurrently) and Algebra II (or concurrently)
courses.notes: *Year-long; dual-enrollment option with River Valley Community College (3 college credits)

courses.description: Grade 10-12 MythBusters is designed for students who want to investigate the scientific validity of many popular beliefs including: myths, rumors, traditions, and stories in a variety of different ways. Students will be presented with various scenarios throughout the semester. They will then learn the science behind the scenario and develop their own models to test whether the outcome is valid or not. The culminating project will be a scenario of their own choosing, presentation of the science behind the scenario, and a model busting or supporting the myth presented.

Forensic Science is a one-semester, interdisciplinary science course that explores methods for collecting, examining, and analyzing various pieces of evidence used in a court of law. Students will use their background in biology, physics, and chemistry to analyze and present evidence clearly and cohesively. Topics include: What is Forensic Science, Collection and Preservation of Evidence, Fingerprint Identification, Forensic Pathology, Forensic Anthropology, Forensic Serology, DNA Fingerprinting, and Forensic Toxicology.

Coastal and Marine Ecology is designed for students who wish to get a better understanding of the environments in and around oceans. Students will investigate the marine environment and its biotic diversity with the major goal of understanding the major groups of organisms, their adaptations, ecological importance and interactions. Dissections will accompany the survey of the 5 major classes of marine invertebrates. The ecology of various marine communities, including but not limited to, estuaries, coral reefs and rocky intertidal zones will also be reviewed. There will be a heavy emphasis on the environmental and conservation efforts to help preserve some of the more delicate coastal and marine ecosystems.. By enrolling in this course, there is the potential to take a March Intensive trip to engage in authentic research centered around marine ecology. Completing this trip will allow you to earn at least 0.5 Flexible Pathways credits.
courses.prerequisites: Prerequisites include successful completion of Biology with a 3.25 or higher and successful completion of Algebra II or concurrent.
courses.notes: Potential March Intensive trip; completing it can earn at least 0.5 Flexible Pathways credits

courses.description: This course will focus on the fundamentals of genetics and evolution. Genetics will begin with a review of Mendelian genetics and move to more complicated human genetics including gene expression and regulation. Evolutionary concepts include the process of natural selection and speciation and the role of genetics in the origin of new species and the diversity of life.
courses.prerequisites: Prerequisites include successful completion of Biology with a 3.25 or higher and successful completion of Algebra II or concurrent.

courses.description: cooking, food, and food ingredients. The relationship between the molecular structure and the function of proteins, carbohydrates, and fats will be examined. Other topics will include chemical reactions during cooking, diets, vitamins, and food additives. This course is supplemented with laboratory experiences. Nutritional Chemistry is designed for college bound students and/or students
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Biology

courses.description: Design and Technology is a semester-long course that offers students a hands-on approach to designing and building products which help societies live a higher quality of life. Students will explore such topics as residential wiring, renewable energy, Computer Assisted Design, Python programming, 3D printing and the engineering design process. Students will learn the fundamentals of hand and power tool safety, as well as their proper usage.
courses.notes: Also listed under Fine Arts (page 47) with identical text

courses.description: Spanish I is designed for beginning language students. The class focuses on acquisition of introductory vocabulary and common phrases as well as basic grammar skills. The class is conducted 75-80% in Spanish and asks students to take risks, make mistakes, and participate in the classroom community without speaking English. Students will learn to negotiate confusion and communicate through use of familiar vocabulary, circumlocution, and physical action instead of defaulting to English. The course is enriched with many geographical and cultural features of Latin America.

This course expands linguistic skills acquired in the first year. Speaking and listening skills are developed as well as grammatical skills necessary for more complex reading and writing. We will broaden our knowledge of high frequency vocabulary on basic topics and deepen our study of verbs, and basic grammatical structures. The class is conducted 85-90% in Spanish and asks students to actively take risks, make mistakes, and participate in the classroom community without speaking English. Like Spanish 1, students will actively work to negotiate confusion and make their meaning known through use of familiar vocabulary, circumlocution, and physical actions. The course is enriched with cultural study focusing on Spain.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (2.5 or higher) in Spanish I or equivalent instruction

courses.description: This course is conducted 85-90% in Spanish with the exception of complicated instructions. Spanish III reviews and continues linguistic skills acquired in the previous levels. The emphasis is interpersonal communication, reading and writing skills, and deepening knowledge of complex grammatical structures and verb forms. Cultural emphasis is placed on Costa Rica, environmental awareness and news from around the world. Students may be eligible to participate in a Cultural Immersion Program.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (2.5 or higher) in Spanish II or equivalent instruction

courses.description: Spanish IV provides advanced study in the Spanish language. The course is conducted entirely in Spanish with the exception of some complex grammar instruction. The students will continue to improve their skills in speaking, listening, reading and writing. Literature, speaking, and writing are stressed in this course. Cultural emphasis is placed on Ancient history, culture, and modern art. Students may be eligible to participate in a Cultural Immersion Program.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion (2.5 or higher) in Spanish III or equivalent instruction

courses.course_name: American Sign Language I Part A (ASL)
courses.description: Students will focus on mastering the basics of fingerspelling, numbers, colors, facial grammar and sentence structure; students will also learn conversational/cultural behaviors necessary to hold a beginning-level conversation in ASL, with Deaf/hard-of-hearing native users of the language.
courses.notes: *Fall Semester Course

courses.course_name: American Sign Language II Part B (ASL)
courses.description: American Sign Language 2 goes beyond introductory ASL signs. This course helps Course students form structured sentences and explores how expressions can enhance signs to have meaningful conversations. Students will learn to communicate in everyday situations while learning vocabulary for descriptions, directions, jobs,
courses.prerequisites: Must have taken ASL Part A
courses.notes: *Spring Semester Course

courses.description: This traditional class focuses on fitness and conditioning, skill acquisition as it relates to individual and team sports, lifetime activities, and a wide range of recreational games. Students will also be participating in the Cooper Institute Physical Fitness Testing program, which evaluates strength, endurance, agility and flexibility. Students are required to come to class dressed appropriately for these athletic activities. Student assessment will be based on rules and strategy knowledge, participation and effort, and sportsmanship.

Students will experience a variety of personal fitness activities including yoga, crossfit, weightlifting and cardio-vascular workouts. Students will design and implement individualized Personal Fitness Plans.

Vermont is a beautiful state with distinct seasons that allow for a variety of outside activities. Students will engage in hiking, snowshoeing, primitive shelter building, orienteering and other outdoor activities. If you love being outside in all of Vermont’s Seasons, this is a class to consider.
Students who play on a varsity sports team may receive .25 PE credit per semester. Maximum of .5 ( 2 semesters)
courses.notes: .25 PE credit per semester, maximum .5 (2 semesters)

courses.description: This class allows students to gain confidence, flexibility and stamina for presentation through dance and core physical work especially geared for performers and athletes. Students will receive training in Lotte Berke, Stott Pilates and mixed martial techniques and explore dance styles for period plays, Broadway and global fusion. Students wishing to take the class must be prepared to move as required, wear suitable clothing and be supportive of themselves and each other.
courses.notes: Also listed under Fine Arts / Performing Arts (page 47, 0.5 credit, Fine Arts Elective/PE, grades 9-12, prerequisite None, can only be taken once) with a different description: "This class allows students to gain confidence, flexibility and stamina for presentation through physical work that will benefit performers." Recorded once, with the page 43 text

courses.description: Students gain the knowledge and skills to make informed decisions about their health and wellness. Along with nutrition and mental health, students will explore topics including healthy relationships, sexual health & substance use.

This studio course allows students to explore their creativity through different mediums and methods. It includes a blend of skill building whole group instruction and lots of opportunities for choice with additional instruction that ranges from direct instruction, facilitated instruction and independent and self-directed learning. This is an open studio format course where students will have the opportunity to explore a wide variety of materials, both 2D and 3D, while focusing on artistic and creative habits, with artists working independently and collaboratively in multiple media in the same studio setting. Students will be required to set learning goals and maintain a digital or physical portfolio to document their growth as artists. All levels of art skill/interest are welcome!
courses.notes: Visual Arts

courses.description: This course focuses on the fundamentals of digital photography. The students will learn how to use three basic concepts: aperture, shutter speed and ISO to manipulate their camera to achieve the desired effects in their photos. Students will work to see the world through the lens of a camera and understand the basics of photographic constructs, and make connections with experts in the field. This is a participatory course requiring students to actively take frequent photos, both indoors and out, to hone their craft.
courses.notes: Visual Arts

courses.description: Students will explore the continuum of furniture making. From the country charm of rustic furniture to the highly sculpted works of Sam Maloof to the utterly bizarre of Gary Knox Bennett. Furniture can shape the environment that we live in and affect how we interact with materials. Students will design and build furniture that reflects their environment and the styles of such masters as James Krenov, Wharton Esherick, Orville Gibson and George Nakashima. Woodworking skill, using both power tools and hand tools will be taught, with an emphasis on quality and aesthetic. Additionally students may explore the trade of being a luthier as they build a guitar.
courses.notes: Visual Arts. Fine Furniture level II is open to students who have successfully completed level I

courses.description: This class allows students to present a formal production before school and community audiences. Students will acquire skills to create theater, to perform and to evaluate performance, and to practice proper terminology and respect for the work of the ensemble.
courses.notes: Performing Arts. Students are required to attend tech week and all performances.

courses.description: This course explores the evolution of theater from its origins in ancient religious rituals to the dynamic, diverse stages of the 21st century. Students will investigate how theater reflects the political, social, and cultural climates of its time. Through reading plays, analyzing historical stagecraft, and engaging in creative projects, students will discover how human beings have used live performance to tell their stories across different eras and continents.
courses.notes: Performing Arts

courses.description: This hands-on course introduces students to the foundational skills, concepts, and equipment used in technical theater and live event production. Students will learn how a show goes from a script on a page to a fully realized production on the stage. Through practical application and collaborative projects, students will explore the primary disciplines of stagecraft, emphasizing safety, creative problem-solving, and teamwork.
courses.notes: Performing Arts. Students are required to attend tech week and all performances.

courses.description: High School Band will be offered to high school students in grades 9-12. Students will focus on the fundamentals of rehearsal etiquette, breathing and air support, mature tone production, embouchure placement, precision of rhythm and tempo, uniformity of articulation and intonation throughout the ensemble. Students will also explore the concepts of musicality by addressing appropriate phrasing, improving on dynamic contrast, and the purpose of emotion in performing musical literature. Students in the concert band are required to perform in all school concerts, any chamber projects, and community events involving the pep band or marching band, and all contests and festival performances.
courses.prerequisites: Minimum 3 years of band experience or Teacher recommendation. Contact Bryan Stammelman for more info.
courses.notes: Performing Arts

courses.description: High School Choir will be offered as a continuing course of study for students wishing to perform in a vocal ensemble. If you like to sing, and are looking to sing with other people, this ensemble is for you! Students will be taught appropriate tone quality, breath support, pronunciation, vocal blend, sight-reading and ear training. Students will rehearse literature as a full ensemble in preparation for performances throughout the school year. Students are expected to participate in all rehearsals and performances for full credit.
courses.notes: Performing Arts

courses.description: Driver Education is designed to develop and/or improve knowledge, skills and attitudes in the safe operation of motor vehicles. It is made up of two parts: (1) classroom phase and (2) behind-the-wheel phase. The course provides 30 clock hours of state-required classroom instruction and six hours of in-car instruction and training. The course meets the requirements for Vermont State certification as well as standards set by insurance companies for rate reduction.
courses.prerequisites: A *Vermont Learner’s Permit is required PRIOR to the start of the course.
courses.notes: Not a graduation requirement; Pass/Fail course, grade not counted towards GPA; sub-contracted through the State of Vermont; NH students need additional behind-the-wheel hours

courses.description: The Career Pathway Project is designed to prepare students for the type of work that they would like to do upon leaving high school and entering into the next steps of their lives. The Career Pathway Project reflects the proficiencies provided by the Portrait of a Graduate initiative and champions the desire for growth that serves as its impetus. This project involves an in-depth exploration of a student-chosen subject with minimum restrictions, in a direction that is new to the student. SWARM time and time outside of school will be focused on helping the student plan, manage, and complete an independent project. The Career Pathway Project involves an in-depth exploration of a student-chosen subject, with minimum restrictions, in a direction that is new to the student. Teacher-advisors serve as facilitators and managers to help the student develop the skills necessary to successfully complete a project of this type. The project must involve work with adults outside of Windsor School; these may be mentors, interviewees, or professionals observed at work. Periodically, students present their progress and product development to their teacher-advisors or to a small panel, along with their interpretations of the meaning and application of that research.
courses.notes: Year-long project in grade 11 (grades 11 & 12 assigned); 12th grade Class of 2026 completes it as seniors

courses.description: A shortened day, full credit program that allows our learners to meet graduation requirements, while offering the flexibility on how to do that. Through this program, open to grades 11 and 12, students will earn credits in the 4 core academic areas (mathematics, science, ELA, and social studies) through a combination of direct teacher instructions, outdoor learning, group projects, experiential learning, field trips and professional learning opportunities. Students will eat lunch, after which they may be dismissed OR work with the school on elective opportunities including in person classes, job shadowing and flexible pathways.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Vermont’s Dual Enrollment Program was created by the Vermont Flexible Pathways Bill, which allows eligible high school juniors and seniors, who are Vermont residents, to take up to two college courses at approved colleges/universities within the state of Vermont. (One course per year during junior and senior year. A course taken during the summer is considered part of the next school year.) Students who successfully complete these courses earn both high school and college credit for each course. This program has an application process, which involves the student, the high school and the college. A key consideration is determining the student’s ability to be successful taking a college-level course while in high school. This determination will be made by the high school and is based on the student’s grades, attendance, work ethic/history, etc. The high school principal is the final approval authority for an application.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Seniors in good academic standing can apply to the Early College Program at one of the Vermont State Colleges. Students apply to the Early College Program at a given college in the spring of their junior year and, if accepted, complete all remaining graduation requirements by taking classes at that college their senior year. Tuition is paid for by the state of Vermont. If a student attends college at a school that is beyond commuting distance, the student can apply to live on campus but is responsible to pay for room and board. Full details can be found on the Vermont Agency of Education site: Early College Vermont AOE .
courses.notes: program

courses.description: This is learning that is delivered through web-based platforms that employ a variety of digital tools, content and supports, and allows for student choice around time, place, pace and content. Students enroll in high school level online classes with or without outside instructors that do not fall under Dual Enrollment or the Early College Program.
courses.credits_text: Credit will be awarded according to the specific option chosen and is determined by the provider of the course.
courses.notes: program. Examples: Virtual High School; Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative (VTVLC); Virtual Learning Academy Charter School (VLACS) (NH Residents only); self-directed options without an assigned instructor (Khan Academy, Coursera, Saylor Academy, MIT Open Courses, other MOOCs)

courses.description: Extended Learning Opportunity (ELO) is defined as any learning that happens outside the traditional classroom that has a set of Learning Goals and Expectations. ELO’s may or may not happen during the school day and within the calendar school year. They can fit the definition of what is called “anytime, anywhere” learning. ELO’s allow students the opportunity to earn credit for learning opportunities that they may already be involved in or would like to take advantage of outside of school. ELO’s offer authentic ways for students to engage in their own learning and collaborate with a community of adults to help them achieve their goals and explore their interests. All ELO’s have a focus on Goals and Learning Expectations that the students will follow as specified in their own plan. All ELO’s will include components of assessment and presentation of learning. ELO’s can also include components of research, reflection, and product and may be a blend of academic content and learning expectations. Students can expect to possibly conduct research, self-monitor their progress, reflect on their learning by various means, collect evidence of their learning, and take part in a culminating presentation at the end of their studies. Students will co-create their Extended Learning Opportunity Plan with a Flexible Pathways facilitator. The plan will identify the academic learning goals the student is hoping to achieve, the learning expectations students will focus on, as well as specify student responsibilities. Students are encouraged to design and or create a plan that meets their learning interests and needs.
courses.credits_text: Credit will be predetermined collaboratively by the Flexible Pathways Committee and the student’s school counselor prior to the student beginning the ELO.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: There may be instances where the opportunities a student needs to fulfill their pathway towards graduation exist within our current Program of Studies. These opportunities generally exist as course electives. When students can identify a series of electives that support their post-secondary plans, they are able to use those electives to satisfy the Flexible Pathway requirement. The connection between the series of electives and the student’s post-secondary goals must be articulated in writing and approved by the student’s school counselor, and Flexible Pathways Committee. Students are encouraged to end their series of electives with a culminating experience that accesses one of the other Flexible Pathway options such as an ELO, CBL, WBL, Online Learning, Dual Enrollment or Early College experience.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Community Based Learning (CBL) provides learners a “learning-by-doing” experience utilizing the community as an extension of the classroom. Community based learning combines meaningful service to the community with the student’s learning goals. Students apply what they learn to a valuable, significant and necessary service to their community. Through mentoring provided by community partners, the learner’s experiences expand beyond high school walls; their perspectives on themselves as engaged young adults and responsible community members change and mature. Community Based Learning is open to all learners who have room in their schedules to be out in the community on a regular basis or who are willing to do their CBL outside of school time. Like Extended Learning Opportunities, there are set Learning Goals and Expectations that are articulated in a plan. Community Based Learning opportunities require and encourage students to be in charge of their own learning as well as collaborate with a Community Partner. CBL opportunities are about hard work, independence, perseverance, collaboration, communication and many other traits employers are looking for in our graduates. Windsor High School is committed to helping students be successful in this type of environment, especially helping them navigate relationships with community partners. Although similar to ELO’s in process, ELO’s generally engage student in preexisting learning opportunities, whereas with CBL, the student is in charge of collaboratively creating the learning opportunity.
courses.credits_text: Credit will be predetermined collaboratively by the Flexible Pathways Committee and the student’s school counselor prior to the student beginning the CBL opportunity.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Experiences in which students can interact with industry or community professionals in real, virtual or simulated work environments that expose learners to post-secondary options, provide opportunities for skill development and allow students to reinforce their school based learning. Work Based Learning is an educational program or experience that offers students an opportunity to reinforce and deepen their learning, explore career fields, and demonstrate their skills. These opportunities particularly help students make the connection between academic principles and real world applications. There are two broad categories within Work Based Learning: Career Exploration and Career Preparation. Career Exploration opportunities provide more focused experiences in which students take a proactive role in identifying and pursuing relevant career and postsecondary options to shape their long-term goals. Once students have a deeper understanding of the world of work, they are able to shape their own pathway in preparation for their chosen careers. Career Preparation experiences are learning opportunities in a workplace that enable students to demonstrate progress towards academic and career/technical proficiency through experiences that are directly related to a specific occupation or trade.
courses.credits_text: Credit will be predetermined collaboratively by the Flexible Pathways Committee and the student’s school counselor prior to the student beginning the WBL opportunity.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: Independent studies are offered to students that may want to take a class that isn’t currently offered or which is an extended version of a class that a Windsor High School teacher offers. In an Independent Study a cooperating content teacher helps determine the curriculum and learning goals the student needs to meet. Independent Study courses require and encourage students to be in charge of their learning and are about hard work, independence and perseverance, many of the traits employers are looking for in our graduates. Students need to be highly self-motivated, self-directed, and able to work independently with limited support in order to be successful in an Independent Study course.
courses.credits_text: Credit will be predetermined collaboratively by the Flexible Pathways Committee, the student’s school counselor and cooperating teacher prior to the student beginning the I.S. course.
courses.notes: program
